subject: chemistry-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Electron configurations
themeLabel: Models of the particulate nature of matter
islUnits: 1. Atomic theory and kinetic theory (Y12 Sep)
bigPicture: Electrons sit in fixed energy levels. When an excited electron drops to a lower level it emits a photon of one exact energy, which is why atoms give line spectra. Levels split into s, p, d and f sublevels, filled in a set order, and the electron configuration that results explains ionization energies and much of the periodic table.

keyIdeas.cue: How are emission spectra produced, and how do colour, wavelength, frequency and energy relate?
keyIdeas.answer: Heating or an electric discharge excites electrons to higher levels; when they fall back they emit photons whose energy equals the gap between levels. Higher frequency = shorter wavelength = higher energy (violet > red; UV > visible > IR). A continuous spectrum contains all wavelengths (white light); a line spectrum shows only specific wavelengths, unique to each element.

keyIdeas.cue: What does the hydrogen emission spectrum show?
keyIdeas.answer: Separate lines prove electrons occupy discrete energy levels. Transitions down to n = 1 emit UV, down to n = 2 emit visible light, down to n = 3 emit IR. Lines get closer together at higher energy because the levels themselves converge. You do not need the series names.

keyIdeas.cue: How many electrons can each main level hold?
keyIdeas.answer: Maximum 2n²: n = 1 holds 2, n = 2 holds 8, n = 3 holds 18, n = 4 holds 32.

keyIdeas.cue: What are sublevels and orbitals; what do s and p orbitals look like?
keyIdeas.answer: Each level splits into sublevels s, p, d, f of increasing energy. An s orbital is spherical; the three p orbitals are dumbbells along the x, y and z axes, at right angles. Sublevel capacities: s 1 orbital (2 e⁻), p 3 (6 e⁻), d 5 (10 e⁻), f 7 (14 e⁻).

Aufbau: fill lowest energy first (1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p). Pauli: max two electrons per orbital, opposite spins. Hund: in a sublevel, occupy orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing. Write full (1s²2s²2p⁶…) or condensed ([Ar]4s²) forms up to Z = 36 and show orbital (arrow-in-box) diagrams. Exceptions: Cr [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ and Cu [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹.

keyIdeas.cue: How is first ionization energy found from a spectrum (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: At the convergence limit the lines merge: the electron has been given enough energy to leave the atom (n = ∞). Use E = hf or E = hc/λ for the convergence frequency or wavelength to get the energy per atom, then multiply by NA and divide by 1000 for kJ mol⁻¹. Trend: first IE rises across a period (higher nuclear charge, same shell) and falls down a group (outer electron further away and more shielded).

keyIdeas.cue: What do successive ionization energies tell you (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: Each successive IE is larger (removing from an increasingly positive ion). A very large jump appears when an electron is removed from a new, inner shell. The number of electrons removed before the first big jump equals the number of valence electrons, which gives the group (for main-group elements).

keyTerms.def: Wavelengths of light emitted as excited electrons fall to lower levels.
Only specific wavelengths; evidence for discrete energy levels.
Region of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron; holds up to two electrons.
Group of orbitals of equal energy within a level (s, p, d, f).
Frequency at which spectral lines merge; corresponds to ionization.
Energy to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms.
Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly before pairing.

workedExamples.title: Configuration of an ion
workedExamples.prompt: Write the condensed configuration of Fe and Fe³⁺ (Z = 26).
steps: When transition metals ionise, 4s electrons are lost first.

workedExamples.title: IE from convergence (AHL)
workedExamples.prompt: The convergence limit of the hydrogen spectrum (transitions to n = 1) is at 91.2 nm. Calculate the first IE of hydrogen in kJ mol⁻¹.

misconceptions.wrong: Electrons absorb energy when they drop to a lower level.
misconceptions.right: Dropping to a lower level releases a photon; absorption moves the electron up.

misconceptions.wrong: 3d fills before 4s, so it also empties last.
misconceptions.right: 4s fills before 3d, but in transition-metal ions the 4s electrons are removed first.

misconceptions.wrong: Hydrogen lines get further apart at higher energy.
misconceptions.right: They get closer together and converge, because the energy levels converge.

checkpoints: Each line = electron transition between two fixed levels

paper1A.stem: Which electron configuration is correct for Cu (Z = 29)?
paper1A.why: Copper is an exception: a full 3d sublevel and 4s¹.

paper1A.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons in the n = 3 level?
In the hydrogen spectrum, which transition emits visible light?
paper1A.why: Drops to n = 2 are visible; n = 1 is UV; n = 1 → 2 is absorption.
Big jump after the first electron: one valence electron.

paper1B.data: Successive ionization energies of element R (kJ mol⁻¹): 1st 578, 2nd 1817, 3rd 2745, 4th 11577, 5th 14842.
paper1B.prompt: Plot or inspect log(IE) against electrons removed. Deduce the group and give the condensed configuration if R is in period 3.
paper1B.answer: Jump between 3rd and 4th → 3 valence electrons → group 13; period 3 → aluminium, [Ne]3s²3p¹.

errorHints.hint: Learn Cr and Cu exceptions and that 4s empties before 3d in ions.
Convert nm to m (× 10⁻⁹) before E = hc/λ, then use NA and ÷1000 for kJ mol⁻¹.
h, c and NA are in the booklet: copy them exactly with units.
Explain IE trends using nuclear charge, distance and shielding; for O vs N use electron-pair repulsion, not 'half-filled stability'.
